$comment: The splash: what the page covers and the ordered list of sections with one-line descriptions. Prose only; the figures it mentions are cited where they appear in the sections.

sections.label: Deployments
sections.title: Deployments and contracts
sections.blurb: Houston has the most mapped Flock cameras of any city. In Texas, a $1 insurance fee helped pay for at least 3,200 before the governor paused state funding.

sections.label: Inside
sections.title: Inside the enclosure
sections.blurb: Fourteen parts in a case 8.75 inches long. The camera reads plates with its own processor and sends each read over a cellular connection.

sections.label: Data
sections.title: Data path
sections.blurb: An alert reaches officers in 10 to 15 seconds on average, Flock says. Reads are kept seven days by default for new customers.

sections.label: Journey
sections.title: Where the picture goes
sections.blurb: One read followed like a parcel through seven stops, from the pole to deletion: what is in the package, who can open it and how long it takes.

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.title: What the reads produce
sections.blurb: Few agencies publish what their cameras produce, and those that do count reads, alerts and arrests differently.

sections.label: Claims
sections.title: Common claims
sections.blurb: Common claims about the cameras, from the company and its critics, checked against the public record.

sections.label: Economics
sections.title: Economics
sections.blurb: A camera lists at $3,000 a year, and Flock keeps the hardware. Installation, permits, moves and replacements cost extra.

sections.label: Sources
sections.title: Sources
sections.blurb: Every document cited on the site, from Flock’s own to court records, with the date each was last checked.
